title: Computing Education in the Era of Generative AI
authors: Paul C. Denny; James E. Prather; Brett A. Becker; James Finnie-Ansley; Arto Hellas; Juho Leinonen; Andrew Luxton-Reilly; Brent N. Reeves; Eddie Antonio Santos; Sami Sarsa
source_used: arXiv author version 2306.02608v1 (accepted CACM version); the ACM DL PDF link (oa_url) returned an HTML page, not a PDF. Page numbers refer to the arXiv PDF.
ft_reason: HE introductory programming; academic integrity and the effectiveness of existing assessments under code-generation LLMs is a substantial section (Sec 2.2) alongside opportunities; refereed CACM review article, 2024.
study_design: Conceptual/review article summarising the authors' own prior empirical studies (Codex on CS1 exam questions and Rainfall variants; LLM-generated exercises and code explanations) plus wider literature
country: Multinational authors (New Zealand, USA, Ireland, Finland); summarised exam study from University of Auckland (New Zealand)
sample: Not applicable for the article overall; the summarised exam study compared Codex with 71 CS1 students on two Python exams; 350 Rainfall responses; 240 generated exercises
genai_tools: OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, GPT-4 (also mentions AlphaCode, CodeWhisperer)

key_findings.finding: Codex scored 78.5% and 78.0% on two real CS1 Python exams, ranking 17th of 71 students (top quartile), though it struggled with tasks that banned certain language features or needed inferred ASCII formatting.

Codex produced highly varied solutions to the same prompt, and common code-plagiarism detection tools are reported to be ineffective against AI-generated code, undermining similarity-based integrity checks.
Authors anticipate institutional shifts to secure assessment conditions and possible use of keystroke/activity data, and question where acceptable machine-generated code ends and misconduct begins.
Suggested assessment shifts include judging style/quality across multiple correct solutions, critique of AI-generated solutions, specification-focused tasks and rewarding incremental testing.
Authors conclude many existing assessment approaches may no longer be effective and argue educators must incorporate the tools and teach responsible use.

dimensions.authenticity: Argues the professional reality of AI-assisted coding should shape tasks (reading, testing, refactoring AI code).
dimensions.capability_verification: Codex reaching top-quartile CS1 exam scores shows typical programming assessments may no longer verify individual capability.
dimensions.integrity_security: Plagiarism detectors are reported ineffective on AI code and AI use is low-risk compared with contract cheating; secure conditions anticipated.
dimensions.lo_alignment: Questions whether code-writing outcomes remain appropriate; argues code literacy (read, test, verify) stays essential.
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Raises the unresolved question of which machine-generated code suggestions are acceptable and how attribution should work.
dimensions.scalability: Notes LLMs could generate a near-endless supply of novel exercises, reducing the cost of fresh assessment items.
dimensions.workload: Generating exercises/explanations with LLMs may reduce instructor effort; filtering poor outputs is still required.
dimensions.process_visibility: Mentions keystroke data and incremental test-writing as possible ways to evidence student process.
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Notes bias in generated code and comments, and greater access for learners without formal education.

author_recommendations: Get ahead of the tools and incorporate them into classrooms from the start, teaching responsible use (not tested)
Shift assessment toward judging quality/style across multiple solutions and critiquing AI-generated code (not tested)
Use specification-focused tasks and renewed test-driven development with rewards for incremental testing (not tested)
Teach the wider societal, legal and ethical implications of generative AI (not tested)
limitations: Not explicitly stated. The article reflects early-2023 models (Codex) and largely summarises prior studies; integrity proposals are speculative.

quality.note: Conceptual review grounded in the authors' empirical studies and cited literature; summarised studies only briefly described; no limitations section.

title: Themes in the Declared Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Assessment
authors: Joseph Maguire; Rosanne English; Qi Ping Cao; Chee Kiat Seow
source_used: University of Glasgow Enlighten repository PDF (eprints.gla.ac.uk/344038), found via OpenAlex locations; CC BY 4.0 version of record. Printed proceedings pages 17-20.
ft_reason: HE computing course; assessment redesign requiring GenAI declarations is the primary focus; peer-reviewed ACM CEP paper; published Jan 2025 (record year 2024), English.
study_design: Practice/experience report with qualitative review of student GenAI declarations (themes identified; analysis procedure not detailed)
country: UK/Singapore (University of Glasgow transnational programme with Singapore Institute of Technology)
discipline: Computing science (digital forensics / cyber security course)
sample: More than 140 students in 37 teams (3-4 members); 74 submissions; 29 teams declared GenAI use
genai_tools: ChatGPT, Grammarly, Phind, Google Gemini, GitHub Copilot

key_findings.finding: Teams could use GenAI but had to declare, for each interaction, the system, rationale, prompt and output, modelled on Monash University guidance.
29 of 37 teams declared GenAI use; ChatGPT was most common, and several teams used multiple tools for different purposes.

Four themes emerged: written quality; research assistance and knowledge building; legal, privacy and ethical concerns; presentation and script creation. One team also used AI to judge its work against the rubric.
Authors interpret GenAI as mostly a starting point rather than a shortcut, and argue declarations help educators check that the assessment measures what was intended.

dimensions.authenticity: Scenario-based team tasks (designing a forensic process for a fictional healthcare organisation; critiquing an investigation).
dimensions.capability_verification: Declarations reveal some teams used GenAI to produce parts of the written submission, which bears on whose capability is assessed.
dimensions.integrity_security: Declaration replaces prohibition; 8 teams declared no use and this was assumed true, so non-declaration was not verified.
dimensions.lo_alignment: Declarations are used to judge whether the assessment assesses what the setter intended and to refine it.
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Students were permitted to use GenAI openly with structured disclosure (system, rationale, prompt, output).
dimensions.feasibility: The approach was implemented in an existing intensive block-mode course without redesigning the tasks.
dimensions.process_visibility: Declared prompts and outputs gave educators visibility of how students approached the assessment.
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Background notes paid GenAI tiers may advantage some students, likened to more sophisticated calculators.

author_recommendations: Educators in computing outside programming may consider asking students to declare and explain GenAI use (not tested beyond this single course)
Use declarations to reflect on and continually refine assessments rather than to make them AI-resilient (not tested)
limitations: Single course in a single institution run in block mode; team-level declarations; no formal analytic method described; self-declaration not verified.

quality.note: Short experience report; theme derivation method not described.

title: Reinventing assessments with ChatGPT and other online tools: Opportunities for GenAI-empowered assessment practices
authors: Dennis Foung; Linda Lin; Julia Chen
source_used: Hong Kong Polytechnic University institutional repository (ira.lib.polyu.edu.hk/bitstream/10397/110034) copy of the published CC BY-NC-ND article, found via OpenAlex.
ft_reason: HE course with assessments redesigned to incorporate GenAI and other AI tools; assessment redesign is the primary focus; peer-reviewed 2024 journal article.
study_design: Qualitative study: thematic analysis of student written reflections and focus group interviews
discipline: English communication course; students mostly from hard sciences incl. engineering, computing, biochemistry
sample: 74 student reflections; 4 focus groups with 28 students; summer semester 2022-23
genai_tools: ChatGPT (3.5), Grammarly (incl. Premium), WeCheck! (in-house), QuillBot, Just The Word, Thesaurus

key_findings.finding: Assessments were redesigned using four features (multimodal, context-specific, learner-specific, multi-source), removing components answerable directly by GenAI and adding personal-experience and lecture-content requirements.

Students had to reflect on their use of AI tools as part of a writing assessment worth 45%; 456 coded items yielded four themes: perception/use, critical evaluation, limitations, and versions of tools.
Students used GenAI for planning and drafting and other tools for grammar/style, and showed critical selection of tools and awareness of wrong information and fake citations.
Students appreciated explicit instructions and in-class demonstrations on constructive GenAI use and linked them to constructive use.
Differences between free and paid tool versions raised equity concerns; authors suggest institutions provide premium access.

dimensions.authenticity: Learner-specific and context-specific requirements tied tasks to personal experience and course content.
dimensions.integrity_security: The redesign aimed to remove components for which GenAI could directly supply answers.
dimensions.lo_alignment: Assessment was redesigned to pursue writing and AI-literacy aims while permitting tools.
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Students were openly allowed and trained to use GenAI and other AI tools constructively and to reflect on their use.
dimensions.feasibility: Redesigned assessments had been run for two semesters.
dimensions.process_visibility: Required reflections showed how tools were used at each writing stage.
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Free vs premium versions created a perceived digital divide; low-proficiency EFL students felt tools levelled the field.

author_recommendations: Adopt a balanced approach allowing flexible use of various AI tools in assessments (supported only by perceptions in this study)
Institutions provide premium versions of AI tools to all students to ensure equity (not tested)
Integrate AI literacy into HE curricula (not tested)
Re-formulate assessment policies so assessments become opportunities to practise using AI (not tested)
limitations: Single course with SYA students of similar language proficiency limits generalisability; the interviewer was a course instructor and the interviewer/coder could influence results; no performance outcome data.

quality.note: Clear qualitative design with two data sources and author verification of coding; limitations stated.

title: Online assessment in the age of artificial intelligence
ft_reason: HE online exam integrity with ChatGPT and exam-help platforms, plus strategies including for CS/coding questions; peer-reviewed case study 2024.
study_design: Single-instructor retrospective observational case study of exam grade distributions, plus in-exam item-modification experiments and experience-based recommendations
discipline: Mathematics/statistics; upper-level machine learning course with programming (R)
sample: Introductory statistics large lecture of 120-150 students per semester (2020-2021 online semesters); upper-level ML course of 20-30 students; exact n per exam not reported
genai_tools: ChatGPT (3.5/4); also third-party homework/exam assistance platforms

key_findings.finding: Unproctored online multiple-choice exams produced markedly higher grades than the same exams in person; reusing an old exam online gave a distribution where A was the most common grade.
When a parameter was changed so the old correct option became wrong, on average 72% of students chose the previously correct answer, indicating reliance on exam-help platforms.
The ChatGPT-specific evidence is one example: ChatGPT solved a standard dice question but failed a modified version; most quantitative data predate ChatGPT.
Recommendations for online exams: no question reuse, tight time limits, screening questions in ChatGPT, and using graphics/unusual symbols; the author notes this adds preparation effort.
For coding questions, require executable code using only taught constructs, with possible follow-up oral explanation, or cap marks for non-compliant code.

dimensions.authenticity: Concludes assessment should shift from rote recall toward analysis, application and synthesis.
dimensions.capability_verification: Proposes calling students in to explain code that goes beyond the constructs taught.
dimensions.integrity_security: Shows unproctored online exams were heavily compromised; lockdown browsers can be bypassed and malfunction for about 2-3% of students.
dimensions.lo_alignment: Course-specific vocabulary and taught constructs used to anchor questions to course teaching.
dimensions.scalability: Strategies were applied in a large lecture of 120-150 students using automated MC grading.
dimensions.workload: Integrity measures need substantial extra question-writing effort, traded against saved grading time.
dimensions.feasibility: Lockdown browser issues required special accommodations and instructor availability during exams.
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Notes harder/shorter exams risk penalising honest students, and lockdown failures affect students through no fault of their own.

author_recommendations: Never reuse exam questions; write new or parameter-modified items (partly tested via in-course experiments)
Impose strict exam time limits to deter live tutoring (not formally tested)
Screen exam questions with ChatGPT and replace those it answers correctly (not tested)
Require executable code limited to taught constructs, with oral explanation if in doubt (not formally evaluated)
limitations: Author acknowledges an observational design without randomisation and alternative explanations (e.g., better home study). Further: single instructor, no inferential statistics, ChatGPT evidence is anecdotal, and the abstract's pre/post-ChatGPT framing is not matched by the data (mainly pandemic-era).

quality.note: Observational grade comparisons without statistical testing; ChatGPT claims rest on a single example.

title: Impact of ChatGPT on learning outcomes and performance of students in computer programming courses: a mixed-method approach
authors: Omobola O. Gambo; Olabamiji John Onifade; Wasiu. Olanrewaju-Smart; Odianose John Abuya; Rukayat Enitan Salawu; Rhodes Massenon; Ishaya Gambo
ft_reason: Primary focus is ChatGPT's effect on learning outcomes, perceptions and scores; assessment design/validity and integrity are only touched on through a few instructor items (reliance, code similarity) and future-work remarks, not a substantial focus.
study_design: Cross-sectional mixed methods: student survey (40 items), instructor survey, course scores; descriptive, correlation, OLS regression and thematic coding
discipline: Computer programming (Python) course across Science, Technology, Environmental Design and Management, and Education faculties
sample: 1889 invited, 1200 responded, 855 valid student responses; 17 instructors; 2023/2024 second semester

key_findings.finding: Students reported positive perceptions (enjoyment mean 3.93, motivation 3.75, confidence 3.72 on 5-point scales).
ChatGPT-related perceptions did not predict programming scores (R2 = 0.006, no significant predictors).
Instructors strongly agreed that students rely on ChatGPT solutions without understanding them (mean 4.29) and often saw significant similarities in submitted code (mean 3.94).
Authors call for new assessment frameworks that can separate genuine understanding from AI-assisted outputs.

dimensions.capability_verification: The gap between perceived usefulness and scores, plus instructor reports of reliance without understanding, suggests assignments may not verify capability.
dimensions.integrity_security: Instructors report frequent code similarity across submissions and integrity concerns; not directly measured.
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Calls for guidelines on responsible use and structured integration of ChatGPT.
dimensions.scalability: Large cohort of 1889 students across four faculties.

author_recommendations: Develop assessment frameworks that distinguish genuine understanding from AI-assisted output (not tested)
Use assignments that require students to critically evaluate, refine or justify AI-generated content (not tested)
Conduct experimental/longitudinal multi-institution studies (not tested)
limitations: Authors note cross-sectional design, self-report bias, single institution and course, few instructors, low R2, non-normal residuals and ceiling effects. Also, it is unclear how anonymous survey responses were linked to scores, and Sec 3.7.5 overstates effects given the non-significant regression.

quality.note: Linkage of scores to the anonymous survey is unclear; some interpretations (Sec 3.7.5) are not supported by the non-significant results.

title: How should we change teaching and assessment in response to increasingly powerful generative Artificial Intelligence? Outcomes of the ChatGPT teacher survey
authors: Matt Bower; Jodie Torrington; Jennifer W. M. Lai; Peter Petocz; Mark Alfano
ft_reason: Most respondents are university teachers (222/318); how assessment should change under GenAI is a primary research question; peer-reviewed 2024 journal article.
study_design: Mixed-methods survey: general linear models on Likert impact ratings; inductive thematic analysis and UTAUT2-coded motivations with inter-rater reliability
country: International (Macquarie University, Australia-led; respondents from the Americas, Australasia, Europe, other)
discipline: Mixed (Arts & Humanities 71, Life Sciences 14, Physical Sciences 40, Social Sciences 129, Technology 59)
level: Mixed: 222 university, 82 high school, 14 primary teachers

key_findings.finding: 61% of respondents rated GenAI's impact on assessment as major (38%) or profound (23%); only 7% said none.
Greater awareness of GenAI predicted higher perceived impact (an 'ignorance effect'); gender, region and teaching level also influenced perceived impact.

Suggested assessment changes: higher-order thinking (n=71), more supervision/invigilation (n=69), authentic tasks (n=65), process focus (n=50), personalised tasks (n=35), spoken tasks such as mini-vivas (n=29), exams (n=21).
54 respondents proposed embedding AI in assessment, e.g., students drafting with ChatGPT and then showing how they improved the draft.
Over 70% of motivations to change assessment were performance expectancy, mainly for students; authors stress the suggestions are perceptions, not evidence of efficacy.

dimensions.authenticity: Authentic tasks were the third most frequent suggested assessment change (n=65).
dimensions.capability_verification: Spoken tasks/mini-vivas and invigilated exams proposed to confirm students' own work.
dimensions.integrity_security: Teachers' proposed changes were driven by plagiarism/unauthorised AI-use concerns, with a widespread call for more supervision.
dimensions.lo_alignment: Higher-order and critical thinking emphasised in redesigned assessment content.
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Some teachers proposed integrating AI into tasks, with students showing how they enhanced AI drafts.
dimensions.workload: Some teachers expected AI to make assessment and feedback more efficient (effort expectancy n=15).
dimensions.process_visibility: Process-focused assessment (drafting, research booklets) suggested by 50 respondents.
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Literature review notes unequal access to AI may widen gaps for disadvantaged groups; not a survey finding.

author_recommendations: Provide teacher professional learning on AI for assessment, built around performance-expectancy motivations (not tested)
Shift assessment toward in-person/invigilated, authentic, personalised, higher-order tasks with source disclosure (teacher perceptions, not tested)
Research the efficacy of teacher-proposed GenAI design patterns (not tested)
limitations: Self-selected social-media sample, not representative; small subgroup sizes; exploratory results; suggestions are perceptions only; early-2023 data (GPT-3.5).

quality.note: Rigorous mixed methods with reported kappa; HE not isolated in all analyses.

title: Can you spot the bot? Identifying AI-generated writing in college essays
authors: Tal Waltzer; Celeste Pilegard; Gail D. Heyman
ft_reason: HE academic integrity: whether instructors can detect ChatGPT-written essays, with implications for assessment; peer-reviewed 2024.
study_design: Pre-registered online experiment (AI Identification Test of 6 essay pairs) with attitude survey (Study 1) and repeated ChatGPT sessions (Study 2)
discipline: Psychology essays; instructors from psychology and other subjects incl. computer science
sample: 140 college instructors and 145 undergraduates (Study 1, Mar-Apr 2023); 40 ChatGPT sessions (Study 2); stimuli from 50 students' proctored exam essays

key_findings.finding: Instructors identified the ChatGPT essay 70% of the time, students 60% and ChatGPT itself 63%; all above chance but far from reliable.
key_findings.location: p. 8 / Study 1 Results; p. 11 / Study 2 Results

key_findings.finding: Neither ChatGPT experience nor subject expertise improved accuracy; general pre-test confidence did not predict performance, but item-level confidence did.
Instructors found pairs with higher-graded student essays harder to tell apart from ChatGPT text.
ChatGPT reported much higher confidence than humans and overestimated its performance by about 28%.
Authors are sceptical of AI detection tools because they are imperfect and false accusations cause harm; they favour redesigning assessments and incentivising cognitive engagement.

dimensions.capability_verification: Instructors cannot reliably tell student writing from ChatGPT writing, so unsupervised essays cannot verify authorship; some instructors suggested pairing writing with oral exams.
dimensions.integrity_security: Provides evidence that ChatGPT poses a significant threat to essay-based integrity; both human and ChatGPT-based detection are unreliable.
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Instructors and students rated direct submission very bad, edited AI essays bad, and AI-generated practice problems good; both groups wanted guidance.
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Non-native English speakers used ChatGPT more and viewed the vocabulary-improvement use more positively.

author_recommendations: Avoid relying on AI detection tools, including asking ChatGPT, to identify AI writing (not tested beyond ChatGPT self-detection)
Develop and share assessment designs that incentivise cognitive engagement and teach AI use as a problem-solving tool (not tested)
Provide clear institutional guidance on acceptable AI uses (not tested)
limitations: Convenience/snowball sample; psychology essays only; student essays were handwritten in exams and lightly corrected; unedited ChatGPT text; unclear why instructors outperform students.

quality.note: Pre-registered design with open materials and appropriate statistics.

title: Work in Progress: Integration of AI Tools on an Open-Ended Computer Programming Project
source_used: Abstract via OpenAlex metadata; no legal OA copy found (OpenAlex closed; no Semantic Scholar record; web search found no author or repository copy). Extracted from the abstract only.
ft_reason: HE intro programming; assessment design allowing AI on an open-ended project while banning it on homework; peer-reviewed FIE work-in-progress paper 2024. Extracted from the abstract only.
study_design: Work-in-progress innovative practice paper describing course assessment design with grade comparisons (details not reported)
country: USA (University at Buffalo, from author affiliations)

key_findings.finding: AI was banned for structured weekly homework (easily solved by AI) but encouraged for an open-ended code-design project judged harder for AI to complete.
Students who reported AI use used it to start the project or part of it and to help with debugging.
Project grades were similar to previous years; midterm two (after the project) scores were higher than midterm one and previous years, but authors do not know whether the project caused this.

dimensions.integrity_security: Structured homework judged vulnerable to AI solutions, which motivated the ban.
dimensions.lo_alignment: AI permission was tied to task type, with the project's learning objective focused on code design.
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Differentiated rules: no AI on homework, AI encouraged on the open-ended project.

author_recommendations: Reuse the AI-integrated open-ended project in future semesters (not tested beyond first implementation)
Collect data on how AI use in the project supports learning (planned)
limitations: Abstract only; work in progress; no causal attribution of the exam improvement; sample and methods not reported.

title: CAP: AI-Augmented Curriculum-Aware Platform for Code Evaluation
authors: Rekha Chaturvedi; Kalpana Mishra; Preeti Sharma; Abhay Sharma; Anubhava Srivastava
source_used: Abstract via Semantic Scholar API (no abstract in OpenAlex); no legal OA copy found (OpenAlex closed; no Semantic Scholar OA PDF; web search found no preprint). Extracted from the abstract only.
ft_reason: Programming education platform for AI-assisted code evaluation and integrity monitoring (code-aware proctoring); HE assumed from the academic programming context and author affiliations (not explicit in abstract); IEEE conference 2026. Extracted from the abstract only.
study_design: System design and technical evaluation (prototype platform tested on standard programming tasks against existing tools)
genai_tools: AI reasoning components with retrieval-augmented code comparison (specific models not reported)

key_findings.finding: CAP combines heuristic static analysis, retrieval-augmented code comparison and real-time editor feedback for formative, curriculum-aligned code evaluation.
It links behavioural proctoring features to code activity for context-aware integrity monitoring.
Authors report better feedback relevance, fewer false positives and efficient real-time performance than existing analysis tools (metrics not given in the abstract).

dimensions.integrity_security: Code-aware proctoring links behaviour to code activity; lower false positives reported.
dimensions.lo_alignment: Evaluation is explicitly aligned to the curriculum rather than to competitive programming.
dimensions.scalability: Modular microservices architecture with real-time performance reported.
dimensions.process_visibility: Monitors in-editor code activity during work rather than only final submissions.

author_recommendations: Use curriculum-aligned AI-assisted code evaluation combined with code-aware proctoring (evaluated only on standard tasks per the abstract)
limitations: Abstract only; prototype; evaluation details, sample and HE deployment not reported; privacy implications of proctoring not discussed in the abstract.

title: A Framework for Assessment Design in the Era of Generative AI: Case Study of Take-Home Assignment in Software-related Courses
authors: Anna Lyza Felipe; Ushik Shrestha Khwakhali; Thanh Ngoc Nguyen
source_used: Abstract via OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar; no legal OA copy found (closed in OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar; web search found no author or repository copy). Extracted from the abstract only.
ft_reason: HE software courses (BIT/BSE); framework for GenAI-era take-home assignment design that preserves integrity; IEEE conference framework paper 2025. Extracted from the abstract only.
study_design: Framework development with a case study of three courses; described as an experimental approach with qualitative analysis
country: Vietnam (RMIT Vietnam, from author affiliations); one author at University of Wollongong
discipline: Information technology / software engineering (BIT and BSE programs)
sample: Three selected courses; student numbers not reported

key_findings.finding: Proposes a framework for take-home assignments in software courses that incorporate GenAI while promoting integrity and curbing plagiarism.
The framework recommends designing assessments at Bloom's taxonomy levels 3-6 to integrate GenAI while keeping integrity and alignment with course learning objectives.

dimensions.integrity_security: Aims to curb AI-enabled plagiarism in take-home assignments.
dimensions.lo_alignment: The framework explicitly ensures alignment with course learning objectives via Bloom's levels.
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: The framework integrates GenAI into assignments rather than banning it.

author_recommendations: Design take-home assignments at Bloom's levels 3-6 to integrate GenAI while preserving integrity (evaluation details not reported in the abstract)
limitations: Abstract only; method, sample and evaluation outcomes not reported.
